stories.headline: South Korea's top scorer in tax accountancy exam admits cheating
stories.script: Our lead story today. The person who came top in South Korea's certified tax accountant exam has confessed to cheating with a tiny camera, a mobile phone and AI tools, the BBC reports. Han Won-seok, who is 34, made the admission in a video posted on Sunday to the YouTube channel of his lawyer, Lee Don-Ho. He said he had also confessed to the Seoul Metropolitan Police Agency and told officers how he did it. In the first round, Han scored 397.5 out of 400, getting only one of 160 questions wrong. That result raised suspicions and set off speculation online. "I cheated in both the first and second rounds," Han said, adding that he had relied on electronic gadgets and generative AI.

stories.headline: Asian governments react to Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s exit
stories.script: Turning to the United States. Governments across Asia have reacted in different ways to Jensen Huang's exit from Nvidia, TechCrunch reports. Some have moved to reaffirm their commitments on chip supplies. Others are watching for any effect on local projects or are dealing with investigations that are still under way. On Sunday, November 8, Nvidia's board opened an independent inquiry following reports that Huang had been the target of a Chinese spying operation. Nvidia's reach extends well beyond America. It has close relationships with firms around the world, especially in Asia, where many of its main partners play central roles in the AI industry. In China, the foreign ministry on November 10 dismissed claims that a Chinese businesswoman connected to Huang was a spy, calling the allegations groundless and a smear against Beijing.
stories.whyThisMatters: Governments across Asia have reacted in different ways to Jensen Huang's exit from Nvidia, TechCrunch reports.
keyPoints: Asian governments react to Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s exit

stories.headline: The AI graveyard: a running list of projects and startups that didn’t make it
stories.script: In other news. TechCrunch is keeping a running list of artificial intelligence products and startups that have failed. Last month the chatbot platform Character.ai filed for bankruptcy only five years after it launched. A few weeks ago, the privacy-focused AI assistant Ollie said it was shutting down. Many AI projects never get beyond the companies that develop them. S&P Global Market Intelligence estimates that about 42% of corporate AI initiatives are eventually dropped. The reasons include a lack of funding, technical hurdles, competition, trouble scaling up and simply weak demand from users. The list covers notable AI launches, startups and bets that have closed, changed direction or fallen well short of expectations. The publication describes it as a record of lessons the wider industry might learn, rather than a tally of failures.
stories.whyThisMatters: TechCrunch is keeping a running list of artificial intelligence products and startups that have failed.

stories.headline: Confucius4-R2T2: A Stable-Prefix Streaming ASR Model for Real Real-Time Transcription
stories.script: And now, our research story of the week. Researchers have introduced a speech recognition system built so it never goes back and changes words it has already produced. Their paper is titled Confucius4-R2T2: A Stable-Prefix Streaming ASR Model for Real Real-Time Transcription. ASR stands for automatic speech recognition, and streaming means the transcript is generated while someone is still talking. Live captions, translation software and voice assistants increasingly act on each word the moment it appears. When a recognizer later revises an early word, a problem sometimes called flicker, any work built on it is wasted, and an AI agent might even take the wrong action. The researchers argue that this kind of stability matters just as much as accuracy and speed. To tackle it, they took an existing model, Qwen3-ASR-1.7B, and gave it further training on 1,500 hours of Chinese and English audio, leaving its core audio-processing components frozen. The method rests on an idea they call the Longest Stable Prefix, essentially the opening stretch of a transcript that can safely be committed without later correction. They provide mathematical proof that this measure behaves consistently and matches what the model would output after hearing the complete recording. Training on these labels turns a model designed for finished recordings into a stable live transcriber, with no change to its underlying design. In testing, the system came close to the original model's quality on full recordings while producing steady text with little delay. The improvements also carried over to languages beyond the two used in training.
stories.whyThisMatters: Researchers have introduced a speech recognition system built so it never goes back and changes words it has already produced.
